heuristics.rule: If you are an Indian national on H-1B with an approved I-140 in EB-2 or EB-3, treat your green card timeline as 50–100+ years under current policy, not as a near-term event
heuristics.condition: When an Indian national is planning their US stay assuming a green card will eventually arrive on a reasonable timeline
heuristics.action: Reframe the immigration timeline as effectively permanent temporary status and make career and life decisions accordingly
heuristics.because: With 525,000+ approved petitions and only ~40,000 visas available annually, the queue is structurally impossible to clear in a human lifespan under current law

heuristics.rule: If you are an Indian national seeking a green card in the US, evaluate EB-1A or EB-5 first, not EB-2 or EB-3
heuristics.condition: When an Indian national is deciding which green card pathway to pursue
heuristics.action: Assess eligibility for EB-1A (extraordinary ability) or EB-5 (investor) before defaulting to employer-sponsored EB-2/EB-3
heuristics.because: EB-1A and EB-5 currently have no per-country backlog for India, meaning a 2–3 year or 4–12 month path versus a projected 134-year path

heuristics.rule: Use O-1A as a bridge visa while building toward EB-1A if you are an Indian national stuck in H-1B dependency
heuristics.condition: When an Indian national wants to decouple their US work authorization from employer H-1B sponsorship and the EB-2/EB-3 queue
heuristics.action: Pursue O-1A classification to remove H-1B cap and lottery constraints while accumulating extraordinary ability evidence for EB-1A
heuristics.because: O-1A is renewable indefinitely, has no per-country backlog, and directly builds the evidentiary record needed for EB-1A self-petition

heuristics.rule: When modeling your US career trajectory as an Indian national, never count a future green card as a planning assumption unless you are on EB-1A or EB-5
heuristics.condition: When making long-term financial, career, or family decisions that assume eventual permanent residency
heuristics.action: Run your life plan assuming the green card never arrives and evaluate whether that plan still makes sense
heuristics.because: EB-2 India priority dates are at May 2012 — meaning even people who filed 12+ years ago are still waiting — making any forward projection speculative

decision_factors.why_it_matters: The difference between EB-2/EB-3 and EB-1A/EB-5 for Indian nationals is the difference between a 100+ year wait and a 2–4 year path — it fundamentally changes whether staying in the US is viable
decision_factors.how_to_assess: Determine current I-140 category; check whether extraordinary ability or investor criteria could be met; get a legal opinion on EB-1A eligibility

decision_factors.why_it_matters: Your priority date determines where you are in the queue; a 2012 priority date means 12+ years have passed and you still cannot file — this is the single most concrete measure of how trapped you are
decision_factors.how_to_assess: Compare your priority date against the current Visa Bulletin cut-off date for your category and country; calculate the gap in years

decision_factors.factor: Nationality (India vs. China vs. all others)
decision_factors.why_it_matters: Per-country caps create wildly unequal wait times despite identical legal treatment — an Indian national faces 134-year EB-2 backlog while most other nationalities face 1–5 years
decision_factors.how_to_assess: Simply identify passport country; Indian and Chinese nationals require completely different analysis than all others

decision_factors.factor: Family size and dependent visa status
decision_factors.why_it_matters: Each dependent consumes one visa slot from the same per-country annual quota — a family of 4 uses 4 slots, effectively quadrupling the personal cost of the backlog
decision_factors.how_to_assess: Count total family members who would need to be included in the green card application; multiply by the annual visa slot cost

decision_factors.why_it_matters: A spouse's ability to work in the US legally depends on the principal's I-140 approval and H-1B stage — if the principal loses their job, the spouse's work authorization is also at risk
decision_factors.how_to_assess: Determine whether spouse holds H-4 EAD; assess whether principal's I-140 is approved; model the household income risk if principal is laid off

decision_factors.why_it_matters: H-1B holders cannot freely change employers without restarting certain processes; AC21 portability helps but has conditions — this creates career ceiling effects independent of skill
decision_factors.how_to_assess: Assess whether AC21 conditions are met (I-140 approved 180+ days, same or similar occupation); evaluate how many career moves have been foregone due to visa constraints

decision_factors.factor: Legislative risk and policy change probability
decision_factors.why_it_matters: Visa recapture acts or country-neutral allocation could dramatically accelerate priority dates — but Congress has repeatedly debated and not enacted these; basing a life plan on legislative hope is high-risk
decision_factors.how_to_assess: Track active legislation; assess historical passage rate of similar bills; treat legislative relief as a low-probability upside, not a planning assumption

decision_factors.why_it_matters: EB-1A bypasses the entire per-country backlog with no employer sponsorship required — it is the primary escape hatch from the EB-2/EB-3 trap for Indian nationals
decision_factors.how_to_assess: Evaluate against USCIS criteria: publications, citations, awards, media coverage, salary relative to peers, judging others' work, memberships in distinguished associations

decision_factors.why_it_matters: EB-5 requires $800K–$1.05M investment but currently has no India backlog — for high-earning Indian professionals with savings or family capital, this may be the fastest permanent residency path
decision_factors.how_to_assess: Assess liquid or accessible capital; evaluate risk tolerance for investment; compare EB-5 processing timeline (4–12 months for rural/TEA) against career and family timeline

decision_factors.factor: Annual fiscal year visa exhaustion timing
decision_factors.why_it_matters: Even approved petitions go unfilled when annual caps are hit — EB-3/EW visas for FY2025 were exhausted by September 9, meaning the practical wait is longer than the queue position alone suggests
decision_factors.how_to_assess: Monitor USCIS Visa Bulletin monthly; track when prior fiscal years exhausted EB-3/EW supply; factor in that exhaustion is recurring, not exceptional

hidden_tradeoffs.choice: Staying in the US on H-1B as an Indian national with an EB-2 or EB-3 I-140 approved
hidden_tradeoffs.unstated_consequence: You are accepting indefinite temporary status — likely for the rest of your working life — with all the career, mobility, and psychological constraints that entails, regardless of how senior you become professionally
hidden_tradeoffs.who_it_affects: High-performing Indian nationals who assume that career success will eventually translate into immigration security

hidden_tradeoffs.choice: Filing an I-140 in EB-2 or EB-3 as an Indian national to 'get in the queue'
hidden_tradeoffs.unstated_consequence: You are not meaningfully progressing toward a green card — you are joining a queue of 525,000+ people competing for ~40,000 annual slots with a 134-year projected wait; the psychological comfort of 'having a petition' is misleading
hidden_tradeoffs.who_it_affects: Indian nationals early in their US careers who treat I-140 approval as a milestone rather than recognizing it is effectively symbolic under current quotas

hidden_tradeoffs.choice: Relying on H-4 EAD for spouse's work authorization
hidden_tradeoffs.unstated_consequence: Household income and the spouse's career are directly contingent on the principal applicant's employment continuity — a layoff triggers a 60-day clock that jeopardizes both people's US status simultaneously
hidden_tradeoffs.who_it_affects: Dual-income households where the spouse has built a career in the US under H-4 EAD and has no independent immigration status

hidden_tradeoffs.choice: Waiting for Congressional legislative relief to solve the backlog
hidden_tradeoffs.unstated_consequence: Visa recapture and country-neutral bills have been repeatedly introduced and not passed — anchoring a multi-decade life plan to low-probability legislation is a structural planning error that forecloses other options over time
hidden_tradeoffs.who_it_affects: Mid-career Indian professionals in their 30s and 40s who have already spent 10+ years in the queue and continue to defer major life decisions waiting for relief

hidden_tradeoffs.choice: Prioritizing EB-2 NIW over EB-1A to avoid PERM complexity
hidden_tradeoffs.unstated_consequence: NIW still carries the full India EB-2 per-country backlog — it only eliminates PERM labor certification, not the 134-year wait. Many professionals choose NIW thinking it is a faster path when it is not
hidden_tradeoffs.who_it_affects: Indian nationals who mistake reduced administrative complexity for reduced wait time

hidden_tradeoffs.unstated_consequence: While AC21 preserves your priority date and I-140 when conditions are met, each job change introduces new risk vectors — conditions must be carefully verified, and a mistake can reset years of queue position
hidden_tradeoffs.who_it_affects: Indian professionals who feel trapped in underperforming jobs or toxic environments and see AC21 as freely enabling mobility

failure_patterns.pattern: Treating I-140 approval as meaningful immigration progress when on EB-2/EB-3 India
failure_patterns.why_it_happens: I-140 approval is a real legal milestone that takes effort and feels significant; most people do not intuitively understand that 525,000 others have the same milestone and only 40,000 slots open annually
failure_patterns.consequence: Professionals build 10–15 year life plans in the US assuming the green card is coming, only to realize mid-career that the wait is effectively infinite under current policy
warning_signs: Describing yourself as 'having a green card pending' without knowing your priority date gap
Making home purchase, family, or location decisions assuming green card arrival within 10 years on EB-2/EB-3 India

failure_patterns.pattern: Defaulting to EB-2/EB-3 employer sponsorship without evaluating EB-1A eligibility
failure_patterns.why_it_happens: EB-2/EB-3 is the standard employer-offered pathway and requires no self-advocacy; EB-1A requires the individual to build and document their own case, which feels uncertain and requires immigration attorney investment
failure_patterns.consequence: Professionals who could qualify for EB-1A spend years or decades in the EB-2/EB-3 queue when a 2–3 year path was available to them
warning_signs: Never having asked an immigration attorney specifically about EB-1A eligibility
Assuming EB-1A is only for Nobel laureates or Olympic athletes rather than senior professionals with publications, high compensation, or peer recognition

failure_patterns.pattern: Planning around legislative relief as a primary strategy
failure_patterns.why_it_happens: Visa recapture and country-neutral bills generate significant media coverage in Indian professional communities; availability heuristic makes passage feel more likely than the historical base rate justifies
failure_patterns.consequence: Professionals defer return-to-India decisions, alternative visa strategies, and major life investments for years while legislation repeatedly fails to pass
warning_signs: Tracking immigration bills closely and citing them as a reason not to pursue EB-1A or EB-5
Having deferred a significant decision ('we'll buy a house when the bill passes') more than once

failure_patterns.pattern: Underestimating the family slot multiplication effect on wait times
failure_patterns.why_it_happens: People naturally think of their own individual place in the queue and do not intuitively model that each family member consumes a separate annual visa slot from the same constrained pool
failure_patterns.consequence: A family of 4 that models a 40-year EB-3 wait is actually in a far worse position per person because their 4-slot consumption means they collectively displace others and worsen aggregate congestion
warning_signs: Citing a backlog estimate without adjusting for family size
Planning to sponsor a spouse for H-4 without modeling what happens if the primary applicant is laid off

failure_patterns.pattern: Ignoring fiscal year visa exhaustion as a recurring structural constraint
failure_patterns.why_it_happens: Annual cap exhaustion in August or September feels like a one-time anomaly rather than a predictable annual pattern; people assume the following year will be different
failure_patterns.consequence: Even professionals whose priority date becomes technically current cannot file because annual supply is exhausted before fiscal year end — the practical wait is longer than the queue model suggests
warning_signs: Monitoring only Visa Bulletin priority dates without tracking annual cap exhaustion timing
Assuming that a current priority date means you can file immediately

diagnostic_questions.question: What is your current I-140 category and country of chargeability?
diagnostic_questions.what_it_reveals: Determines whether you face a 1–5 year wait (most nationalities, EB-1A) or a 40–134 year structural trap (Indian national EB-2/EB-3) — the entire decision framework changes based on this answer
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_yes: If Indian national on EB-2/EB-3: What is your priority date and how does it compare to current Visa Bulletin cut-offs?
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_no: If not Indian or Chinese: What is your current priority date gap and how many years realistically remain?

diagnostic_questions.question: Have you ever had a formal assessment of your EB-1A eligibility from an immigration attorney?
diagnostic_questions.what_it_reveals: Reveals whether the person has explored the primary escape hatch from the EB-2/EB-3 trap; most people who would qualify have never been told they might
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_yes: What criteria did the attorney assess, and what was the outcome? When was this assessment done relative to your current career stage?
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_no: What is your current publication record, salary percentile relative to peers, awards, media coverage, or roles judging others' work? These are the EB-1A evidentiary pillars.

diagnostic_questions.question: Does your spouse work in the US, and if so, under what visa status?
diagnostic_questions.what_it_reveals: If the spouse is on H-4 EAD, the household has a hidden single point of failure — the principal applicant's employment continuity determines both people's work authorization simultaneously
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_yes: Is the H-4 EAD dependent on an approved I-140? What is the household's financial plan if the primary applicant faces a 60-day grace period clock?
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_no: Does the spouse have independent immigration status, or are they currently unable to work? This affects the financial calculus of staying vs. returning significantly.

diagnostic_questions.question: What major life decisions have you deferred because you are waiting for your green card?
diagnostic_questions.what_it_reveals: Surfaces the hidden cost of the wait — if someone has deferred homeownership, children, eldercare for parents, or career moves for 5+ years, they are already paying the 'immigration tax' whether they name it or not
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_yes: How long have these decisions been deferred? What is the compounding cost of continued deferral if the wait extends another 10–20 years?
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_no: Have you fully internalized that EB-2/EB-3 India timelines are 50–134 years under current policy, or are you operating on an assumption of resolution within 10–15 years?

diagnostic_questions.question: Do you have or could you access $800K–$1.05M for an EB-5 investment?
diagnostic_questions.what_it_reveals: Determines whether the fastest current no-backlog green card path is available; for high-earning professionals or those with family capital, this may be a live option that has never been seriously evaluated
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_yes: Have you consulted with an EB-5 attorney about rural or TEA project timelines (4–12 months processing)? How does that compare to your EB-2/EB-3 wait?
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_no: At your current savings rate and compensation trajectory, when would this capital threshold become accessible? Is that timeline competitive with other options?

diagnostic_questions.question: When did you last check the Visa Bulletin, and do you know whether annual EB-3 visas were exhausted before fiscal year end in the last two years?
diagnostic_questions.what_it_reveals: Tests whether the person understands that annual cap exhaustion is a recurring structural problem — not just queue position — that makes practical filing impossible even when priority dates appear current
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_yes: If aware of exhaustion: How have you adjusted your planning to account for the gap between apparent priority date currency and actual ability to file?
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_no: This is a critical gap in understanding your actual timeline — the EB-3/EW cap was exhausted by September 9, 2025 for FY2025 and August 16, 2024 for FY2024.

diagnostic_questions.question: Are you tracking any specific immigration legislation, and has an anticipated bill affected any decision you have made in the last two years?
diagnostic_questions.what_it_reveals: Identifies whether the person is making real decisions based on low-probability legislative outcomes — a major failure pattern that can defer action for years
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_yes: What is your assessment of the historical passage rate of similar bills? What is your contingency plan if the bill does not pass in the next two years?
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_no: Good — are you aware that visa recapture and country-neutral proposals have been debated for over a decade without enactment?

industry_realities.common_belief: If you have an approved I-140, you are on your way to a green card — it's just a matter of waiting
industry_realities.actual_reality: For Indian nationals in EB-2 or EB-3, an approved I-140 means you have joined a queue of 525,000+ people competing for ~40,000 annual slots, with projected waits of 40–134 years. The I-140 is a queue ticket, not a path.
industry_realities.implication: Indian nationals should not make life decisions based on the assumption that their EB-2/EB-3 I-140 will result in a green card within their working lifetime under current law

industry_realities.common_belief: The green card backlog is a temporary problem that Congress will fix
industry_realities.actual_reality: Visa recapture and country-neutral allocation bills have been introduced and debated for over a decade without passage. The backlog has grown, not shrunk, during this period.
industry_realities.implication: Legislative relief should be modeled as a low-probability upside scenario, not a planning assumption — decisions should be made that are sound even if no legislation passes

industry_realities.common_belief: EB-1A (Extraordinary Ability) is only for world-class talents like Nobel laureates, Olympic athletes, or globally famous researchers
industry_realities.actual_reality: EB-1A is available to senior professionals who meet a combination of criteria including above-peer compensation, publications, peer review roles, industry awards, and media coverage — many mid-to-senior level professionals qualify without being globally famous
industry_realities.implication: Any Indian national in EB-2/EB-3 who has not had a formal EB-1A eligibility assessment is leaving open the possibility of a 2–3 year path they have never evaluated

industry_realities.common_belief: India and China face similar green card backlogs because both have large applicant pools
industry_realities.actual_reality: EB-2 India has a projected 134-year wait; EB-2 China has a 5–10 year wait. Despite identical per-country caps, India's applicant volume is catastrophically larger, creating a fundamentally different situation despite equal legal treatment.
industry_realities.implication: Career and immigration advice that is appropriate for a Chinese national on EB-2 (plan around a 7-year wait) is dangerously wrong when applied to an Indian national (plan around an indefinite permanent temporary status)

industry_realities.common_belief: If your priority date becomes current in the Visa Bulletin, you can file for your green card
industry_realities.actual_reality: Annual visa caps are regularly exhausted before fiscal year end — EB-3/EW visas for FY2025 ran out by September 9. A current priority date does not guarantee you can actually file and receive a visa that year.
industry_realities.implication: Effective wait times are longer than queue position alone suggests; planning must account for annual cap exhaustion as a recurring event, not an anomaly

industry_realities.common_belief: EB-2 NIW (National Interest Waiver) is a faster path than standard EB-2 for Indian nationals
industry_realities.actual_reality: NIW only eliminates the PERM labor certification process — it does not affect the per-country backlog queue. An Indian national on EB-2 NIW faces the same 134-year projected wait as one on standard EB-2.
industry_realities.implication: Choosing NIW over standard EB-2 to 'go faster' is a category error — it reduces administrative burden but does nothing to address the fundamental backlog problem

industry_realities.common_belief: A family of 4 Indian nationals waits the same amount of time as a single applicant for a green card
industry_realities.actual_reality: Each family member consumes one visa slot from the same annual per-country quota. A family of 4 uses 4 slots, effectively multiplying the household's impact on and exposure to the backlog.
industry_realities.implication: Backlog wait time estimates that do not account for family size understate the true household-level cost of pursuing EB-2/EB-3 as an Indian national with dependents

industry_realities.common_belief: O-1A is just an alternative to H-1B and does not help with the green card situation
industry_realities.actual_reality: O-1A removes H-1B cap and lottery constraints, is renewable indefinitely, and directly builds the evidentiary record for EB-1A self-petition — making it a strategic bridge toward the only no-backlog path available to most Indian nationals
industry_realities.implication: For Indian nationals who can qualify for O-1A, it is not merely an H-1B alternative — it is the beginning of a deliberate EB-1A strategy that bypasses the entire per-country backlog system

junior_vs_senior_signals.dimension: Understanding of what I-140 approval means
junior_vs_senior_signals.junior_pattern: Celebrates I-140 approval as meaningful progress toward a green card; tells peers 'my green card is in process'
junior_vs_senior_signals.senior_pattern: Recognizes that I-140 approval for Indian nationals on EB-2/EB-3 is entry into a 525,000+ person queue with ~40,000 annual slots — and immediately evaluates alternative pathways
junior_vs_senior_signals.why_it_matters: Misinterpreting I-140 approval as progress leads to a decade or more of deferred decisions based on an immigration outcome that will not arrive

junior_vs_senior_signals.junior_pattern: Uses a single point estimate ('the wait is about 10 years') or accepts employer HR's characterization without verifying against current Visa Bulletin data
junior_vs_senior_signals.senior_pattern: Checks current priority date cut-offs against their own priority date, understands the annual cap exhaustion pattern, and models a range of scenarios including no legislative relief
junior_vs_senior_signals.why_it_matters: Single-point estimates that are wrong by an order of magnitude (10 years vs. 134 years) lead to catastrophically wrong life decisions

junior_vs_senior_signals.junior_pattern: Accepts the pathway their employer offers (usually EB-2 or EB-3) without independently evaluating EB-1A eligibility or EB-5 feasibility
junior_vs_senior_signals.senior_pattern: Proactively seeks an independent immigration attorney assessment of EB-1A eligibility; evaluates EB-5 against current savings trajectory; treats employer-offered pathway as one option, not the only option
junior_vs_senior_signals.why_it_matters: The difference between EB-2 and EB-1A for an Indian national is potentially 130+ years of wait time — not evaluating alternatives is one of the highest-cost passive decisions available

junior_vs_senior_signals.junior_pattern: Monitors immigration bills closely and makes real decisions contingent on passage ('we'll decide when the bill passes')
junior_vs_senior_signals.senior_pattern: Treats legislative relief as a low-probability upside; makes all primary decisions assuming no legislation passes; if relief arrives, treats it as a bonus, not a plan
junior_vs_senior_signals.why_it_matters: Basing multi-year life plans on bills that have repeatedly failed over a decade is a systematic planning error that compounds over time

junior_vs_senior_signals.junior_pattern: Models immigration status at the individual level; assumes spouse's H-4 EAD is stable as long as their own status is stable
junior_vs_senior_signals.senior_pattern: Models immigration risk at the household level; understands that a layoff triggers a 60-day clock that simultaneously threatens both the principal's and spouse's US work authorization
junior_vs_senior_signals.why_it_matters: A household that has two incomes but one immigration anchor is structurally fragile in ways that individual-level analysis does not reveal

junior_vs_senior_signals.junior_pattern: Checks whether their priority date is 'current' in the Visa Bulletin and assumes that means they can file
junior_vs_senior_signals.senior_pattern: Tracks both priority date currency AND annual cap exhaustion timing; knows that EB-3/EW visas ran out in August–September in both FY2024 and FY2025, making apparent currency practically irrelevant for many applicants
junior_vs_senior_signals.why_it_matters: Misreading Visa Bulletin currency as actionability leads to planning errors where professionals believe resolution is closer than it actually is
